claims.statement: EIOPA recognizes that insurers can use product design, underwriting, and pricing incentives to encourage risk prevention, supporting an insurer-controlled mitigation workflow in principle.

EIOPA's insurer pilot found retail implementation early, risk effects hard to standardize, open evidence scarce, and explicit premium discounts uncommon; insurer-supplied loss evidence must precede any savings claim.
EIOPA's public dashboard supplies country and peril context from economic losses, insured losses, risk estimates, and coverage, but not a verified property intervention-to-claim outcome dataset.

Established vendors already offer insurers property-level hazard, damage, underwriting, pricing, and mitigation intelligence, so a startup must control the intervention-evidence workflow rather than compete as a broad catastrophe model.

Polish property cover already links policy terms to maintenance and inspections, while insurance-distribution rules make it prudent for the startup to remain white-label infrastructure under insurer-controlled coverage, pricing, and customer communications.
No gathered evidence shows that a Polish insurer will fund a pilot, expose policy and claims data, accept contractor evidence, or pay the proposed per-policy and per-intervention fees.

contrary_evidence: EIOPA reports that only a few participating insurers used explicit discounts and that precise risk effects are difficult to assess.
Retail insurance contracts are highly standardized, while intervention effectiveness depends on property, peril, and implementation details.
ICEYE and ZestyAI demonstrate well-capitalized competition in insurer property intelligence.
PZU already incorporates maintenance, inspection, prevention content, and policy conditions, creating an internal-build or incumbent-extension threat.

economics.acquisition_route: Ask one insurer or broker to define a single peril, eligible intervention, evidence checklist, and retrospective success measure; build only after a paid pilot and data-access agreement, using a small approved contractor cohort.
economics.founder_net_worth_path: Planning hypothesis, not forecast: 500000 assessed policies at 16 PLN blended annual net revenue would yield 8.0M PLN ARR. At 27% EBITDA, 4x EBITDA, and 60% founder ownership, founder equity would be about 5.2M PLN, plausibly in year 8-11 only after insurer-grade loss evidence and repeatable distribution. Retained cash is not double-counted.
economics.founder_time: 12-18 hours weekly for a paid narrow pilot, with insurer-owned underwriting decisions and contract actuarial, privacy, and insurance counsel.
economics.gross_margin_basis: Planning range of 45-65% during contractor-assisted verification and 65-78% after evidence standards and sampling mature; no gathered evidence validates these margins.
economics.payback: Unknown until an insurer reveals procurement cost, integration effort, policy volume, and avoided-loss measurement; do not spend beyond the bootstrap cap without a paid pilot.
economics.pricing: Pilot a fixed 60000-150000 PLN project; only then test hypotheses of 5-15 PLN per assessed policy annually plus 50-150 PLN per insurer-approved verified intervention.
economics.retention_or_repeat: Quote and renewal cycles recur annually and mitigation status can be refreshed, but renewal and policyholder completion are unvalidated.

fingerprint.compounding_advantage: Insurer-defined, auditable intervention evidence linked under contract to later aggregate claims outcomes
fingerprint.customer: Property insurers or brokers running one narrowly defined prevention program for home or small-commercial portfolios
fingerprint.distribution_mechanism: White-label insertion into insurer quote, renewal, or prevention communications with approved contractors
fingerprint.offer_and_business_model: Insurer-controlled mitigation task workflow, timestamped evidence ledger, contractor sampling, and outcome-analysis feed
fingerprint.payer_and_paid_event: Insurer pays for a scoped pilot and later per assessed policy or accepted evidence record
fingerprint.problem_trigger: An insurer identifies a preventable peril at quote or renewal and has an approved measure whose effect it wants to test

founder_fit: The evidence pipeline and outcome analysis use the founder's quantitative and automation strengths.
The family renewable-energy company offers bounded access to contractor workflow knowledge, not assumed insurer distribution.
One institutional payer can distribute to many policyholders and avoids founder-led consumer marketing.
A contract-gated pilot fits the capital limit and can be performed part-time if underwriting and regulated advice remain with the insurer.
risks: A mitigation record can be mistaken for a safety certificate or guarantee; insurer-approved language and explicit limits are required.
Insurer procurement, data protection, model validation, and claims maturation can make feedback cycles very long.
Contractor evidence may be inconsistent, fraudulent, expensive to sample, or operationally burdensome.
Broad hazard scoring is already served by established property-intelligence vendors.
Insurance advice or distribution activity could trigger duties outside the intended software-provider role.

structure.control_point: Accepted property-level mitigation record tied to insurer-defined eligibility and later outcome analysis
structure.critical_dependency: A payer must supply a narrow intervention hypothesis, policy and claims linkage, and enough volume for credible measurement

thesis: Provide a property insurer with a white-label evidence workflow for one insurer-selected peril and one approved mitigation class. The insurer owns risk selection, policy language, incentives, and underwriting; the product explains the task, captures timestamped contractor evidence, samples it, and returns an auditable ledger for later aggregate claims analysis. It does not sell insurance, promise savings, or invent a property-risk model.
title: Insurer-Controlled Mitigation Evidence Ledger
uncertainties: Which Polish peril and intervention have enough claims frequency, measurable effect, and affordable verification.
Whether an insurer will expose policy, property, intervention, and claims linkage to a small vendor.
What evidence standard an underwriter, claims team, and approved contractor can all support.
Whether policyholders complete tasks without an immediate material incentive.
Pilot procurement time, implementation cost, price, renewal, fraud rate, and gross margin.
